steps.t: Each store runs one zero-touch Socket; its LAN firewall keeps POS apart from guest, staff and IoT.
Broadband carries the store to the nearest PoP; LTE/5G stands by so the tills keep authorising.
Only the POS VLAN reaches the payment processor; guest and IoT get internet-only breakout.
One policy for every store, with events and the Audit Trail as the assessor evidence pack.

steps.t: Sockets at every site terminate the last mile; the EOL firewall estate is retired, not refreshed.
All enforcement runs in the PoP single-pass engine: FWaaS, IPS, anti-malware and TLS inspection.
One global rule base reaches every PoP in seconds; TLS inspection is a policy decision, not hardware.
IPS virtual patching shields the unpatched app server in the DC while ops patch on their own timetable.

One telemetry plane feeds XDR stories, the Audit Trail and Experience Monitoring — the DORA evidence.

steps.t: The Socket passively discovers every plant device — category, type, model, OS, manufacturer — no agents.
Its LAN firewall enforces Purdue-level segmentation on the plant floor from device-attribute rules.
WAN and internet policy is enforced at the PoP: a PLC dialling out to the internet is dropped.
A maintenance vendor reaches only the jump server over ZTNA; every allow and block is an event in the CMA.

steps.t: Every flow from every site, remote user and cloud instance crosses a PoP — there is no unexamined path.
SPACE inspects it once against every engine: SWG, DNS, IPS, NGAM, sandbox, firewall and DLP.
Six kill-chain stages meet six independent controls, from delivery through C2 to exfiltration.
XDR correlates every blocked attempt into one MITRE-mapped incident story in the data lake.

steps.t: The root certificate is deployed fleet-wide and verified on every OS before a single flow is decrypted.
A pilot cohort is inspected first with the downstream engines in monitor, so breakage lands as events.
Inspection expands category by category; pinned and mTLS apps get explicit, owned bypass rules.
QUIC is blocked so browsers fall back to inspectable TCP 443; enforcement is the last gate.
